t: Longest Well-Performing Interval — Prefix Scores and First-Occurrence Hashing
o: Map each day to a score of +1 if hours > 8, else -1. A well-performing interval is a subarray whose score sum is strictly positive, so the task reduces to finding the longest subarray with positive sum. For example 1, scores are [1,1,-1,-1,-1,-1,1]; the subarray [9,9,6] has sum +1, giving length 3. In example 2 all scores are -1, so no subarray has positive sum and the answer is 0. With n up to 10^4, an O(n^2) brute force passes, but an O(n) solution using prefix sums is straightforward once we reframe the problem this way.
k: Convert tiring/non-tiring days into +1/-1 values; the problem becomes 'longest subarray with strictly positive sum'.
For each prefix index j with prefix sum s, the best i is the earliest index where prefix sum equals s-1; any earlier occurrence gives a longer interval.
Store only the first occurrence of each prefix-sum value in a hash map — later occurrences can never yield a longer interval.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force over All Intervals
a.i: Check every pair of endpoints (i, j), maintaining a running count of tiring vs non-tiring days as we extend j from i. Whenever tiring days exceed non-tiring days, update the best length. This directly mirrors the definition and needs no extra insight.
s: For each start index i, reset counters for tiring and non-tiring days.
Extend end index j from i to n-1, incrementing the appropriate counter based on hours[j] > 8.
If tiring > non-tiring, update ans = max(ans, j - i + 1).
a.t: O(n^2) — two nested loops over all interval endpoints.

a.n: Approach 2: Prefix Sum + First-Occurrence Hash Map (Optimal)
a.i: Let prefix[i] be the running +1/-1 score after i days. The interval (i, j] is well-performing iff prefix[j] - prefix[i] > 0, i.e., prefix[i] < prefix[j]. Since consecutive prefix sums differ by exactly 1, the best choice is the earliest index where prefix sum equals prefix[j] - 1; if that value never appeared, no valid earlier index exists. Record only the first occurrence of each prefix value in a hash map, because a later occurrence always yields a shorter interval.
s: Initialize score = 0, ans = 0, and map {0: -1} (empty prefix at index -1).
Iterate over days, adding +1 or -1 to score.
If score > 0, the whole prefix works: ans = max(ans, i + 1).
Else if score - 1 exists in the map, ans = max(ans, i - map[score - 1]).
If score is not yet in the map, record map[score] = i; return ans.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with O(1) average hash-map operations.
a.sp: O(n) — the hash map may hold up to n distinct prefix sums.

a.i: Build the prefix-score array. A candidate left endpoint must be a strict prefix minimum (strictly decreasing stack of indices), since a larger earlier prefix would be dominated by a smaller one further left. Scan right endpoints from the right; pop stack indices while prefix[right] > prefix[stack top], updating the answer — this greedily matches each left candidate with its farthest valid right endpoint.
s: Compute prefix array p of length n+1 with p[0] = 0.
Push indices onto a stack while keeping p strictly decreasing along the stack.
Scan j from n down to 1; while the stack is non-empty and p[j] > p[stack.top()], pop it and set ans = max(ans, j - popped index).
a.t: O(n) — each index is pushed and popped at most once across both scans.
a.sp: O(n) — prefix array plus the stack.

w: In an interview, present Approach 2: the +1/-1 reframing plus first-occurrence hashing is clean, optimal, and easy to justify. Mention brute force first to establish correctness, and note the monotonic-stack variant generalizes to 'longest subarray with sum greater than k' when step sizes aren't ±1. Pitfalls: forgetting the seed {0: -1} for prefixes starting at day 0, using <= instead of strict positivity, and storing last rather than first occurrences of prefix sums (which silently shortens answers). Edge cases: all non-tiring days (answer 0), all tiring days (answer n), and single-day inputs. Follow-ups often ask for the general 'longest subarray with sum > k' version, which requires the monotonic stack approach.
